findings.title: Race condition in device limit enforcement
findings.body: CountDevices and the subsequent decision to insert vs update are not performed atomically. Multiple concurrent requests can all see count < deviceLimit and proceed to INSERT, resulting in more devices than deviceLimit allows. This defeats the purpose of a hard device limit under concurrent load.

findings.title: Device tagging now synchronous, changing authentication latency and failure semantics
findings.body: Previously TagDevice was invoked in a background goroutine with its own timeout so that tagging failures/slowness never affected the Authenticate call path. The change makes TagDevice synchronous and returns errors (notably ErrDeviceLimitReached) directly from Authenticate, meaning every anonymous authentication now blocks on a DB write and that a client exceeding the device limit is fully denied authentication rather than just not being tracked. This is a significant behavior change (anonymous access can now fail entirely once device limit is reached) that should be explicitly called out, and lacks the previous panic-recovery/timeout safety net for a synchronous DB call occurring on the hot auth path.

findings.title: TagDevice error now propagated up through Authenticate, which was previously only logged
findings.body: a.tagDeviceUI's error is now returned instead of only logged with a.log.Debug. Combined with the synchronous call in client.go, any transient DB error during tagging (not just device-limit) will now cause Authenticate to fail for anonymous users, whereas before failures were swallowed. This broadens the blast radius of DB hiccups to break anonymous access entirely.

findings.title: Device limit check doesn't account for existing device being updated
findings.body: When count >= deviceLimit, the code unconditionally calls updateDevice instead of first checking if the device already exists (e.g., a known device checking in again should always succeed via normal upsert, not just within the expiration window check in updateDevice). This conflates 'at limit, so only allow updates to existing active devices' with potential false negatives if a legitimately active device's updated_at narrowly falls outside the window used in the update condition, causing ErrDeviceLimitReached for an existing device instead of updating it via the normal insert-or-update path.
